processing: Very lightly oxidised (around 10–15%), ball-rolled and dried without roasting, in the Li Shan high-mountain style.
harvest_season: Two picks at most: late spring from late May into June, and winter in October.
appearance_dry: Dense, tightly rolled jade-green balls with a waxy sheen and a cool, sweet dry aroma.
appearance_liquor: Pale greenish gold, thick-looking and clear.
appearance_wet: Thick, whole, deep-green leaves on sturdy stems with scarcely any red at the edge.
taste_profile: Cold, clean sweetness with pear and white flowers, a silky body a shade lighter than Fushoushan and a long cooling finish that keeps returning.

brewing.notes: Full dose, boiling water and a long first steep to open the balls; eight or more infusions. Not a tea to pair with anything strong.

vintage_note: The farm sells its own tea by harvest, the June and October picks of the current year, in sealed, labelled packs in limited quantity, mostly on site; sellers elsewhere group 'Wuling' with Li Shan and may mean gardens in the surrounding valley rather than the farm. It is drunk fresh, within a year, never aged.
description:
Wuling is one of the Veterans Affairs Council's mountain farms that put the Lishan area on the tea map: Wuling Farm sits in the Qijiawan river valley in Heping District, Taichung, at roughly 1,750 to 2,100 metres, better known for peaches, apples, cherry blossom and the landlocked salmon in its stream than for tea. Its tea gardens are small, and the oolong they produce is high-mountain tea in the Li Shan style at its most delicate.

The leaf is Qing Xin oolong, very lightly oxidised, ball-rolled and unroasted, picked twice a year at most, in late spring from late May into June and again in October. The valley is cold and shaded for part of the day, so the leaf grows slowly and comes out thick and sweet, and the processing stays out of its way.

The cup is cold, clean sweetness with pear and white flowers, a silky body a shade lighter than Fushoushan and a long cooling finish that keeps returning; it is a quiet tea that rewards attention. Brew it with a full dose and boiling water, give the balls a long first steep, and expect eight or more infusions; it is not a tea to pair with anything strong.

The farm sells its own tea in sealed, labelled packs in limited quantity, mostly on site, and sellers elsewhere group 'Wuling' with Li Shan, sometimes meaning the farm's tea and sometimes meaning gardens in the surrounding valley. Ask which, and expect the farm's own to be scarce. It is sold by harvest and drunk fresh, within a year, never aged.

If you cannot find it, a Fushoushan or a well-sourced Li Shan lot from the same season is the nearest thing.
sources_note: The farm's altitude range and the size of its tea plantings are approximate; I am confident Wuling Farm sells its own high-mountain oolong but less sure how much of the market 'Wuling' tea comes from the farm itself versus neighbouring gardens.
